steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MFBE, a dense bi-encoder retrieval model for FAQ retrieval that uses the multiple fields of an FAQ (question, answer, category). Motivate it from customer support automation and the shortage of labeled training data, and finish with our list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Customer support and why automate it with FAQs
2. FAQ retrieval: problem definition and the lexical gap
3. Lack of labeled query-FAQ data
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Customer support (CS)
- critical to any business: customer retention, new customer acquisition, branding, better experience
- online CS: customers send queries, human agents attend to them
- team of CS agents scales with query volume and agent productivity -> operational cost
- CS automation: automated responses + better agent productivity -> saves cost
- typical approach: auto-respond from repository of FAQs, insulate agents from high query volumes
- success = fraction of queries auto-answered -> depends on user query to FAQ matching

2. FAQ retrieval
- each FAQ = multi-field tuple \langle Q,A,C\rangle: question Q, answer A, question category C
- task: retrieve top-k FAQs for user query q
- lexical gap between natural-language user query and matching FAQs, as in typical retrieval
- usual fix: learn relevance function from labeled query-FAQ pairs

3. Labeled data
- often unavailable or scarce, esp. low-resource settings like Japanese query-FAQ retrieval (our domain of interest)
- manual labeling expensive, needs domain knowledge

4. Contributions
- MFBE: bi-encoder retrieval model using multi-field info (question, answer and/or categories)
- combinations of user query and FAQ fields -> extended set of pseudo-positive pairs for training
- multiple FAQ representations at inference for query-FAQ scoring

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Customer support (CS) is critical for any business. It plays an important role in keeping customers, getting new customers, branding, and giving a better experience. In a typical online customer support setting, the customers send their queries and human agents attend to them. So businesses need to hire and keep a team of CS agents, and this team scales with the query volume and with how productive the agents are, which becomes operational cost for the business. Customer support automation can help save this cost by giving automated responses to queries and by making support agents more productive. One way businesses usually try to do this is to automatically respond to customer queries from a repository of frequently asked questions (FAQs), so that human agents are insulated from high query volumes. How successful such a system is, measured as the fraction of customer queries it responds to automatically, then depends on how well user queries are matched to FAQs.

We have a collection of FAQs, and each FAQ is a multi-field tuple \langle Q,A,C\rangle of question Q, answer A, and question category C. The FAQ retrieval problem is to retrieve the top-k FAQs for a user query q. Like a typical retrieval problem, FAQ retrieval also has the problem of lexical gap between the user query, which is written in natural language, and the FAQs that match it. Usually this is handled by learning a relevance function between user queries and FAQs, with labeled query-FAQ pairs as supervision. But such labeled data is often not available or scarce, especially in low-resource settings like Japanese query-FAQ retrieval, which is the domain we are interested in. Getting large amounts of this labeled data by manual labeling is often expensive and needs domain knowledge to do the labeling.

Contributions (to write up):
- MFBE: bi-encoder retrieval model using multi-field info in FAQs (question, answer and/or categories)
- combinations of user query and FAQ fields -> extended set of pseudo-positive pairs for training
- multiple FAQ representations during inference for query-FAQ scoring

How successful such a system is, measured as the fraction of customer queries it responds to automatically, then depends on how well user queries are matched to FAQs.

Like a typical retrieval problem, FAQ retrieval also has the problem of lexical gap between the user query, which is written in natural language, and the FAQs that match it. - We use multiple FAQ representations at inference time for scoring query-FAQ pairs.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Customer support (CS) is critical to any business and plays an important role in customer retention, new customer acquisition, branding, and in driving a better experience. In a typical online customer support setting, customers reach out with their queries and human agents attend to them. This requires businesses to hire and maintain a team of CS agents that scales with the query volume and the productivity of agents, which translates to operational cost for the business. Customer support automation [1] can help save on this cost by providing automated responses to queries and by improving support agent productivity. Businesses typically try to achieve this by automatically responding to customer queries from a repository of frequently asked questions (FAQs), thereby insulating human agents from high query volumes. The success of such a system, measured as the fraction of customer queries that it automatically responds to, then depends on the effectiveness of user query to FAQ matching.

Given a collection of FAQs where each FAQ is a multi-field tuple \langle Q,A,C\rangle of question Q, answer A, and question category C, the problem of FAQ retrieval [2,3,4,5] is to retrieve the top-k FAQs in response to a user query q. As in a typical retrieval problem, FAQ retrieval suffers from the lexical gap between a user query expressed in natural language and the corresponding matching FAQs. This is typically addressed by learning a relevance function between user queries and FAQs, using labeled query-FAQ pairs for supervision. Unfortunately, such labeled data is often unavailable or scarce, especially in low-resource settings like Japanese query-FAQ retrieval, which is our domain of interest. Curating large amounts of such data through manual labeling is often expensive and requires domain knowledge.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

- We propose a bi-encoder based retrieval model, MFBE, that leverages multi-field information (question, answer and/or categories) in FAQs.

- We use different combinations of user query and FAQ fields to create an extended set of pseudo-positive pairs for training.

- We employ multiple FAQ representations during inference for query-FAQ scoring.

References:
[1] Mesquita, T., Martins, B., Almeida, M.: Dense template retrieval for customer support. In: Proc. of the 2022 Intl. Conf. on Computational Linguistics. pp. 1106–1115
[2] Sakata, W., Shibata, T., Tanaka, R., Kurohashi, S.: Faq retrieval using query-question similarity and bert-based query-answer relevance. In: Proc. of the 2019 Intl. ACM SIGIR Conf. on Research and Development in Inf. Retr. pp. 1113–1116
[3] Dutta, S., Assem, H., Burgin, E.: Sequence-to-sequence learning on keywords for efficient faq retrieval. arXiv preprint arXiv:2108.10019 (2021)
[4] Seo, J., Lee, T., Moon, H., Park, C., Eo, S., Aiyanyo, I.D., Park, K., So, A., Ahn, S., Park, J.: Dense-to-question and sparse-to-answer: Hybrid retriever system for industrial frequently asked questions. Mathematics 10 (8) (2022)
[5] Karpukhin, V., Oguz, B., Min, S., Lewis, P., Wu, L., Edunov, S., Chen, D., Yih, W.t.: Dense passage retrieval for open-domain question answering. In: Proc. of the 2020 Conf. on Empirical Methods in NLP. pp. 6769–6781
